questions.question: At Bletchley Park in 1944, engineers built a programmable electronic machine with roughly 1,500 vacuum tubes to break the German Lorenz cipher — far faster than the Bombes attacking Enigma. Name it.
questions.explanation: Colossus was the wartime codebreaker built for Lorenz, distinct from the Enigma-attacking Bombes.

questions.question: To settle what is computable, a 1936 paper imagined a device reading and writing symbols on an infinite tape, one cell at a time, under a simple table of rules. Name this theoretical model.
questions.explanation: Turing's abstract tape machine formalized the limits of mechanical computation.

questions.question: In 1983 Apple shipped a roughly $10,000 workstation with a mouse, icons, and windows — a year before the cheaper Macintosh popularized the GUI — and named it after Steve Jobs's daughter. Name it.
questions.explanation: The Lisa (1983) was Apple's first GUI computer, preceding the Macintosh.

questions.question: In 1947, Shockley, Bardeen, and Brattain demonstrated a solid-state amplifier at a New Jersey research facility — work that earned a Nobel Prize and eventually replaced vacuum tubes. Name the facility.
questions.explanation: The transistor was invented at Bell Labs in 1947.

questions.question: In May 1997 a purpose-built IBM machine evaluating about 200 million chess positions per second won a six-game match 3.5–2.5 against reigning champion Garry Kasparov. Name the machine.
questions.explanation: IBM's Deep Blue was the first computer to beat a reigning world chess champion in a match.

questions.question: Third-generation machines replaced rows of discrete transistors with single silicon chips containing entire circuits — the breakthrough Kilby and Noyce pioneered around 1959. Which component defines that generation?
questions.explanation: The integrated circuit packs transistors onto one chip and defines third-generation computers.

questions.question: In 1964, Dartmouth professors designed a language so that non-science students could program on a timesharing system, with lines like '10 PRINT "HELLO"'. Name it.
questions.explanation: BASIC was created at Dartmouth specifically as a beginner-friendly teaching language.

questions.question: In 1981 a 24-pound machine with a 5-inch screen, two floppy drives, and bundled software became the first commercially successful portable computer, beating the laptop era by years. Name it.
questions.explanation: The Osborne 1 (1981) is recognized as the first commercially successful portable computer.

questions.question: On January 1, 1983, ARPANET forced every host onto a two-part protocol suite — one part routes packets between networks, the other guarantees ordered delivery — a date now called the Internet's birthday. Name the suite.
questions.explanation: The 1983 ARPANET flag day switched all hosts to TCP/IP, the Internet's foundation.

questions.question: The 1994 Simon — a touchscreen device combining phone, pager, PDA, email, and apps — is regarded as the first smartphone. Which company built it?
questions.explanation: IBM built the Simon Personal Communicator in 1994, predating the modern smartphone era.

questions.question: He designed the CDC 6600 — the first machine called a supercomputer — then founded his own company to build the liquid-cooled, C-shaped Cray-1 in 1976. Name this engineer.
questions.explanation: Seymour Cray designed the CDC 6600 and later the Cray-1, earning the 'father of supercomputing' title.

questions.question: During Apollo 11's descent, this roughly 70-pound onboard computer kept flying the lunar module through 1201 and 1202 program alarms with only about 4 KB of RAM. Name it.
questions.explanation: The Apollo Guidance Computer ran the LM descent, surviving the famous 1201/1202 alarms.

questions.question: In 1971 an experimental program hopped between ARPANET hosts displaying 'I'm the creeper, catch me if you can' — the first self-replicating network program. Name it.
questions.explanation: Creeper was the first known self-replicating program, spreading across ARPANET in 1971.

questions.question: A docent explains that ENIAC's technicians replaced failed components almost daily because every one of its vacuum tubes was a potential failure point across 30 tons of hardware. Roughly how many tubes did ENIAC contain?
questions.explanation: ENIAC's logic ran on about 18,000 vacuum tubes, whose failure rate demanded constant maintenance.

questions.question: His 1948 paper 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' defined the bit and set the theoretical limits of data compression and channel capacity. Name this Bell Labs mathematician.
questions.explanation: Claude Shannon founded information theory, defining the bit and channel capacity.

questions.question: ENIAC filled a room and used about 18,000 vacuum tubes. Which 1947 invention made computers dramatically smaller and more reliable?
questions.explanation: The transistor replaced bulky, heat-prone vacuum tubes and launched second-generation computers.

questions.question: A museum labels machines by generation: vacuum tubes first, transistors second, integrated circuits third. A 1981 PC built around a single-chip CPU belongs to which generation?
questions.explanation: Fourth-generation computers are defined by the microprocessor, which put an entire CPU on one chip.

questions.question: In 1969 engineers linked computers at UCLA, Stanford, UC Santa Barbara, and Utah into a four-node network. Name this direct ancestor of the Internet.
questions.explanation: ARPANET pioneered packet switching between those four sites and evolved into today's Internet.

questions.question: Which 1957 programming language, still used for scientific and engineering computation, was the first widely implemented high-level language?
questions.explanation: Fortran (FORmula TRANslation) proved high-level languages could rival hand-written assembly for speed.

questions.question: In 1991 a Finnish student released a free hobby operating-system kernel that now powers most servers, supercomputers, and Android phones. Name it.
questions.explanation: Linus Torvalds posted the Linux kernel in 1991; combined with GNU tools it became the dominant server OS.
